title: Message Queues and Streaming
tagline: Async decoupling is the backbone of resilient systems — queues and streams let services communicate without waiting for each other.

sections.content:
When Service A calls Service B synchronously, A waits for B to respond. If B is slow, A is slow. If B crashes, A fails. **Message queues** break this coupling: A drops a message into a queue and immediately continues, while B processes it whenever it is ready. This single change converts brittle, latency-chained architectures into resilient, independently scalable services.

Beyond simple queues, **event streaming** platforms like **Apache Kafka** add durability and replay: every event is persisted to disk, consumers can re-read old events, and multiple independent consumer groups can each read the same stream from their own position. Understanding the difference between a queue (each message consumed once by one consumer) and a pub/sub stream (each message consumed by every subscriber group) is fundamental to choosing the right tool for async communication.

sections.caption: A queue decouples producer from consumers. The producer publishes and moves on. Consumers pull messages at their own pace and acknowledge (ack) after successful processing. Unacknowledged messages are redelivered.

sections.title: The Restaurant Ticket System
sections.content:
In a busy restaurant, waiters do not stand in the kitchen waiting for each dish. They write an **order ticket**, pin it to the rail, and go serve other customers. The kitchen reads tickets in order, prepares dishes, and rings the bell when ready. The ticket rail is the **message queue**: it decouples waiter speed from kitchen speed, buffers demand during a rush, and lets the kitchen scale independently (add more cooks) without changing how waiters take orders.

**Kafka** is like a restaurant that keeps every order ticket ever written, filed by table and date, so that a new cook can read back all orders from the beginning of service to understand what happened — and a health inspector can audit the full history even months later.

**Point-to-point queues** (RabbitMQ, SQS, BullMQ) guarantee that each message is delivered to exactly one consumer. This is ideal for task distribution: resize this image, send this email, process this payment. Workers compete for messages; adding more workers scales throughput linearly.

**Pub/sub** (publish/subscribe) broadcasts each message to all subscribed groups. One event — "order.placed" — can simultaneously trigger an inventory service, an email notification service, and an analytics service, each consuming independently. This is the basis of **event-driven architectures**.

**Apache Kafka** is a distributed event streaming platform that combines both models at massive scale. Key concepts:
- **Topic**: a named, partitioned log. Messages are appended to a topic and retained on disk (configurable, often days or weeks).
- **Partition**: a topic is split into ordered, immutable partitions for parallelism. A 12-partition topic can be consumed by up to 12 consumers in parallel within a consumer group.
- **Offset**: each message in a partition has a sequential integer offset. Consumers track their own offset, allowing independent progress and arbitrary replay.
- **Consumer group**: a named group of consumers that collectively read a topic. Kafka assigns partitions across the group — each partition is owned by exactly one consumer in the group.

**Delivery guarantees** are a critical trade-off:
- **At-most-once**: message is delivered without confirmation; may be lost on crash. Fast but lossy.
- **At-least-once**: message is redelivered until acknowledged; duplicates are possible. Consumer must be **idempotent**.
- **Exactly-once**: Kafka supports this with transactional producers and idempotent consumers, but it adds complexity and reduces throughput.

sections.caption: Two independent consumer groups consume the same Kafka topic. Each group maintains its own offset, so the analytics service can lag behind without affecting the notification service, and either can replay from any offset.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Using `order.id` as the message key ensures all events for the same order land on the same partition, preserving per-order ordering even across retries. The consumer's `groupId` is unique per service — a separate analytics consumer group with a different `groupId` reads the same topic independently. If the email send fails and throws, Kafka retries the message (at-least-once); ensuring `sendOrderConfirmationEmail` is idempotent prevents duplicate emails.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Design consumers to be idempotent** — safe to run twice with the same message. At-least-once delivery (the default for Kafka and most queues) means duplicates are possible on retry. An idempotency key check (`setnx` in Redis, or a unique constraint in the DB) lets you accept this trade-off without corrupting data. Exactly-once semantics exist but add significant complexity; prefer idempotent at-least-once in almost every real system.

items: **Message queues** decouple producers from consumers: the producer publishes and moves on; consumers process at their own pace, enabling independent scaling and absorbing traffic spikes.

**Point-to-point queues** deliver each message to one consumer (task distribution); **pub/sub** delivers each message to all subscriber groups (event fanout). Choose based on whether downstream services compete or cooperate.
**Kafka** stores messages durably in partitioned, ordered logs. Multiple consumer groups each track their own offset, enabling independent consumption, replay, and audit at scale.

**Partitions** are the unit of parallelism in Kafka: a topic with N partitions can be consumed by at most N consumers in parallel within one consumer group. Partition keys control which partition a message lands on, preserving ordering per key.
**At-least-once delivery** is the practical default — design consumers to be **idempotent** (safe to process the same message twice) rather than paying the cost of exactly-once transactions.

quiz.question: What is the primary benefit of using a message queue between two services instead of a direct synchronous HTTP call?
options: Message queues are always faster than HTTP for individual requests
The producer is decoupled from the consumer — it does not block waiting for a response
Message queues automatically retry failed HTTP connections
Queues encrypt messages in transit, making them more secure than HTTP
quiz.explanation: With a queue the producer publishes a message and immediately moves on. The consumer processes it asynchronously, at its own pace. This eliminates the latency coupling and failure propagation of synchronous calls.

quiz.question: In Kafka, what is an 'offset'?
options: The number of milliseconds a message is delayed before delivery
A sequential integer identifying the position of a message within a partition
The byte size of a message in the Kafka broker
A consumer group's lag behind the producer in seconds
quiz.explanation: Each message within a Kafka partition is assigned a monotonically increasing offset. Consumers commit their current offset to track progress, and can seek to any offset to replay historical messages.

quiz.question: How many consumers (in the same consumer group) can read from a Kafka topic with 6 partitions in parallel?
options: Unlimited — any number of consumers can read any partition simultaneously
1 — Kafka is single-threaded per topic
6 — each partition is assigned to at most one consumer in a group
3 — half the partition count, as Kafka uses pair-wise assignment
quiz.explanation: Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer within a consumer group at a time. With 6 partitions you can have at most 6 active consumers reading in parallel. A 7th consumer in the same group would be idle, waiting for a partition to become available.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between a point-to-point queue and pub/sub?
options: Point-to-point queues support persistence; pub/sub does not
In pub/sub each message is delivered to every subscriber group; in a queue each message is consumed by one consumer
Pub/sub requires acknowledgement; queues are fire-and-forget
Queues are push-based; pub/sub is pull-based
quiz.explanation: A point-to-point queue distributes messages among competing consumers — each message goes to exactly one. Pub/sub broadcasts each message to every subscriber group, enabling fan-out (e.g., one event triggering multiple independent services).

quiz.question: Why should consumers be designed to be idempotent when using at-least-once delivery?
options: Because Kafka consumers run in parallel and may receive the same message simultaneously
Because at-least-once delivery means a message may be redelivered after a crash, causing duplicate processing
Because message brokers compress duplicate messages into one for efficiency
Because idempotency is required to achieve exactly-once delivery
quiz.explanation: With at-least-once delivery, if a consumer processes a message but crashes before committing the offset, the broker redelivers the message. Idempotent consumers (e.g., using a processed-ID check) handle duplicates safely without side effects.

quiz.question: What happens to messages published to a Redis Pub/Sub channel when no subscriber is currently connected?
options: Messages are stored in a buffer and delivered when the subscriber reconnects
Messages are dropped — Redis Pub/Sub has no persistence or buffering
Messages are stored for up to 24 hours then expired
Redis automatically switches to a durable queue mode
quiz.explanation: Redis Pub/Sub is not durable. If no subscriber is listening when a message is published, the message is silently dropped. For reliable delivery use Redis Streams, a dedicated queue (BullMQ, SQS), or Kafka.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of using a message's key (e.g., order ID) as the Kafka partition key?
options: It compresses the message to reduce broker storage
It ensures all messages with the same key land on the same partition, preserving order per key
It routes the message to a specific consumer by ID
It enables exactly-once delivery for that message
quiz.explanation: Kafka hashes the partition key to select a partition. All messages with the same key (e.g., same order ID) go to the same partition, which is consumed sequentially by one consumer — preserving ordering per entity even at high throughput.

quiz.question: Which delivery guarantee adds the most complexity and reduces throughput in Kafka?
options: At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once
Best-effort
quiz.explanation: Exactly-once semantics require Kafka's transactional producer API and idempotent consumer processing, coordinated across broker and consumer state. This adds latency and operational complexity. Most systems instead use at-least-once with idempotent consumers.

quiz.question: A Kafka topic retains messages for 7 days. A consumer group falls 3 days behind due to a bug fix deployment. What can it do?
options: Nothing — unconsumed messages are deleted after one day
It can reset its offset to any point within the 7-day retention window and replay events
It must request the producer to republish the missed messages
Kafka automatically delivers buffered messages in a batch on reconnection
quiz.explanation: Kafka's durable log retains all messages for the configured retention period. A consumer group can seek to any offset within that window and replay events — a capability not available with traditional queues that delete messages after consumption.

quiz.question: In an event-driven architecture, which scenario is best served by pub/sub rather than a point-to-point queue?
options: Distributing image resize jobs across a pool of worker processes
An 'order.placed' event that must trigger notifications, inventory updates, and analytics simultaneously
Processing payment transactions one at a time to prevent double-charging
Scheduling background database cleanup jobs every night
quiz.explanation: Pub/sub fans out one event to multiple independent subscribers. All three services (notifications, inventory, analytics) consume the same event independently. A point-to-point queue would only deliver the message to one of the three.
